t: #2547 — Minimum Cost to Split an Array
o: Split nums into contiguous subarrays; each part costs k plus the length of the part after deleting values that occur exactly once in it. We minimize the total cost. With n ≤ 1000 an O(n²) DP is expected. For example 1, splitting [1,2] | [1,2,1,3,3] costs 2 + 6 = 8. The trimmed length of a window equals the window length minus the number of values occurring exactly once inside it, which is easy to maintain incrementally as the window grows/shrinks.
k: dp[i] = minimum cost to split the first i elements; transition tries every last-part start j.
Trimmed length of nums[j..i] = (i−j+1) − (number of values with count exactly 1 in the window).
Fixing i and growing the window leftward lets counts be updated in O(1) per step, giving O(n²) total.

a.n: Approach 1: Quadratic DP with incremental window counts
a.i: For each end i, scan j from i down to 0, maintaining a frequency map of the window nums[j..i] and a counter `singles` of values whose count is exactly 1. The candidate cost is dp[j] + k + (window length − singles). Take the minimum over j.
s: Initialize dp[0] = 0 and dp[i] = infinity otherwise.
For each i from 0 to n−1, reset the count map and singles counter.
Extend the window leftward from j = i to j = 0, updating counts and singles in O(1).
Set dp[i+1] to the minimum of dp[j] + k + (i−j+1−singles); answer is dp[n].
a.t: O(n²) — for each of n endpoints we scan back over the whole prefix with O(1) updates; n ≤ 1000 makes this about 10⁶ operations.
a.sp: O(n) for the DP array plus O(n) counts (values are bounded by n).

w: This DP is the standard intended solution; the clever part is maintaining the 'singles' count incrementally instead of recomputing the trim per window. Watch for overflow when k is up to 1e9 (use 64-bit intermediates). A follow-up could ask for the same problem with n up to 1e5, which requires a segment-tree 'DP with history' (Li Chao / Kinetic) technique.
